submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires at the point where a general, characterizing claim - what something is, or is generally like, rather than a report of a one-off event - is grounded or defined, peaking on the connector that carries the relation: 'since', 'as' or 'because' introducing its reason or evidence ('Plants need water since they cannot store it'; 'as' also fires in 'as well as' and evidential 'as shown by'), 'refers to' in a definition, and, more weakly, the period that ends such a claim. It stays inactive when the same words mark time, comparison, exemplification, concession or consequence ('since 2010', 'as big as', 'such as', 'although', 'so'), and when a because/since clause explains a one-off event ('The window shattered because the ball hit it').

adversarial_test_results.prompt: In the spring of 1987 a survey crew of four men reached the northern edge of the Kettle River valley, where a stand of old-growth forest had never been mapped. They carried chains, a theodolite, and a folder of aerial photographs taken the previous autumn. The first three days went badly. Rain turned the access road into mud, and the truck sank to its axles twice before the crew abandoned it and walked in from the highway. On the fourth morning the sky cleared. They laid a baseline along the ridge above the river and began measuring. Every distance had to be checked twice, and the theodolite had to be leveled again after each gust of wind. By noon they had covered barely three hundred meters. The crew camped that night beside a shallow creek. After supper the youngest of them, a student named Hollis, walked up the slope with a lamp and a notebook. He had been asked to record the understory plants along the baseline, a job nobody else wanted. He found ferns in the wet hollows, moss covering the north side of every trunk, and a patch of pale orchids he could not identify. When he came back he showed his sketches to the others, and the oldest man, who had worked in the valley when he was young, said he had seen those orchids only once before, in a bog farther downstream. They argued about the name for a while and then went to sleep. The survey continued for eleven more days. The crew measured the height of the largest trees, noted the depth of the leaf litter, and marked every spring and seep they crossed with a numbered stake. They saw deer tracks in the mud, a porcupine in a hemlock, and once, at dusk, a black bear moving along the far bank. The weather held. Each evening Hollis added new pages to his notebook, and by the end of the second week he had filled more than half of it. Nobody paid him much attention. The others were behind schedule and spent their evenings arguing about the road and the supplies. The report the crew filed that autumn was short, but one paragraph in it drew attention years later. Forests on north-facing slopes hold far more moisture through the dry season than forests on the opposite side of a ridge, because they receive less direct sunlight and lose less water to evaporation. The crew had measured this difference by accident, in the springs and seeps they had been asked to mark, and their notes eventually became the basis for a study that changed how the regional foresters planned their burns. Hollis never published anything himself. He kept the notebook, though, and his daughter donated it to the county archive in 2004.
